tldr: Moving away from shallow-water visual eye candy, this work physically integrates sensor drift, higher-order hydrodynamics, seafloor terramechanics, and deep-sea optical models essential for deep-sea robotics into the Stonefish simulator.
hero_caption: An overall view of the extended Stonefish simulator. In a deep-sea environment reaching depths of up to 10,000 m, it computes buoyancy, gravity, Coriolis forces, Magnus effect-induced lift, depth-dependent density variations, and terramechanical traction/resistance forces for seafloor rovers in comprehensive real time.
overview:
Recent underwater robotics simulators tend to focus heavily on photorealistic rendering powered by modern game engines. However, in the deep sea hundreds of meters down, sunlight caustics from surface waves never reach. Instead, the true challenges are poor visibility under artificial lighting in complete pitch-black darkness, and long-duration sensor drift in GPS-denied environments. The simplistic white noise, static biases, and basic shallow-water hydrodynamic models used in conventional simulators mask the true drift of state estimators. This allows learning-based autonomy algorithms to exploit non-physical simulator artifacts.

To address this, the authors significantly extended Stonefish, an open-source underwater physics simulator, for deep-sea conditions. Specifically, they implemented an IMU model capturing colored noise and thermal drift comparable to real MEMS sensors, a DVL (Doppler Velocity Log) reproducing per-beam measurements and long-term drift, and a magnetometer considering geomagnetic models (WMM/IGRF) along with hard-iron and soft-iron disturbances. In addition, they introduced mesh-based lift forces, the Magnus effect, Coriolis forces, depth-dependent density and added mass variations, and a terramechanics model based on Bekker's theory for seafloor exploration rovers (crawlers).

Validation experiments included Allan variance analysis using real IMU data, 3-hour DVL dead reckoning tests, and CFD comparisons of a lander descending to 3,000 m depth. The results confirmed that the new framework accurately captures long-term cumulative errors and lateral drifts caused by rotation-hydrodynamic coupling, both of which were overlooked by conventional simulators. This provides a practical, reliable platform for navigation and autonomy research grounded in the harsh physical reality of the deep ocean.
contributions: Built a unified stochastic sensor framework faithfully reproducing real IMU Allan variance characteristics (bias instability), long-term DVL drift, geomagnetic inclination, and hard/soft-iron disturbances.

Introduced higher-order hydrodynamic models evaluated per surface mesh face, including lift, the Magnus effect, Coriolis forces, and depth-dependent variations in seawater density (pycnocline) and added mass due to compression.
Integrated a lightweight terramechanics model based on Bekker's pressure-sinkage theory, enabling real-time simulation of seafloor crawler locomotion and touchdown dynamics.
Implemented a camera lens distortion model (barrel and pincushion) and established a ROS bridge with a specialized deep-sea optical renderer (DeepSea) to generate high-fidelity deep-sea imagery.

sections.heading: Why visual-only realism falls short in deep-sea robotics
sections.summary: Many shallow-water simulators lean heavily on visual flashiness from game engines, failing to reproduce deep-sea physics and severe sensor constraints. This section discusses why physical and sensor fidelity matters far more than appearances for deep-sea mission success, outlining the expanded Stonefish framework.
sections.details:
Simulation is vital for developing underwater robotics and evaluating algorithms. Deep-sea missions in particular carry immense costs and risks for field trials, making high-fidelity simulation indispensable. However, many existing underwater simulators (such as those based on Unity or Unreal Engine) primarily target shallow-water AUVs (Autonomous Underwater Vehicles) and ROVs (Remotely Operated Vehicles), placing their emphasis on computer-graphics-driven visual realism.

In the deep ocean, visual phenomena like water-surface caustics and crepuscular rays simply do not exist. What truly governs robot perception and localization in the deep sea are wavelength-dependent light attenuation, severe turbidity, extremely low signal-to-noise ratios, and, in GPS-denied environments, long-term IMU drift and intermittent acoustic DVL measurements.

Simulators relying on coarse physical and sensor models (such as pure Gaussian white noise) conceal estimator bias accumulation and yield overly optimistic control performance. In particular, autonomous AI policies trained via model-free reinforcement learning run the risk of exploiting non-physical simulator quirks and inconsistencies.

To overcome these issues, this work builds upon the open-source rigid-body and fluid simulator Stonefish, proposing a real-time deep-sea simulation framework encompassing stochastic sensor models, higher-order hydrodynamics, terramechanics, and deep-sea optical models.

sections.heading: Limitations of existing simulators and the role of Stonefish
sections.summary: Existing underwater simulators like DAVE, OceanSim, and MarineGym tend to sacrifice deep-sea sensor drift and hydrodynamics in favor of training throughput or visual rendering. This study bridges that gap by enhancing Stonefish, which excels at geometry-based hydrodynamic computation, for deep-sea regimes.
sections.details:
Several simulators have been developed for underwater robotics, but all have faced trade-offs by either prioritizing shallow-water settings or simplifying physics for computational speed.

- ROS-integrated frameworks like DAVE: They offer integrated environments for robot arms and vehicles, but their environmental interactions and sensor models remain basic, limiting applicability to deep-sea conditions.
- Modern GPU rendering simulators like OceanSim: They deliver fast photorealistic image generation and physically based rendering for select sensors, yet their coverage of vehicle dynamics, higher-order hydrodynamic forces, and long-term sensor behavior is limited.
- MarineGym: It prioritizes reinforcement learning training throughput above all else, drastically cutting down on sensor fidelity and environmental physics models.

Conventional Stonefish excelled at hydrodynamic calculations via surface integration over CAD geometry, coupled manipulator dynamics, and ROS compatibility. However, it lacked deep-sea inertial and magnetic drift models, depth-dependent environmental variability, and physically based deep-sea optical attenuation. This work extends Stonefish to elevate its physical and sensor fidelity to true deep-sea standards.

sections.heading: A stochastic IMU model capturing real-world sensor quirks
sections.summary: Replacing conventional white noise and static bias models, the authors propose a stochastic IMU model incorporating axis non-orthogonality, scale factor errors, colored noise, thermal drift, and thruster vibration. Over 9 hours of Allan variance analysis against a real tactical-grade IMU (JIMS-80) confirm realistic bias instability.
sections.details:
In dead reckoning under GPS-denied conditions like the deep sea, minute IMU errors accumulate over time, leading to catastrophic positioning drift. Most conventional simulators only implement Gaussian white noise and static biases, failing to reproduce the long-term fluctuations characteristic of real MEMS sensors.

The proposed model comprehensively integrates the following components:
- Scale factor and axis alignment errors: Captures sensitivity errors and non-orthogonalities across axes using matrices $\mathbf{M}$ and $\mathbf{S}$.
- Stochastic bias drift: Accumulates low-frequency gyro and accelerometer drift modeled as Brownian motion (random walk).
- Time-correlated noise: Incorporates a first-order Gauss-Markov process to reproduce MEMS-specific colored noise.
- Quantization and measurement range limits: Simulates ADC discretization via LSB stepping and saturation limits.
- Temperature-dependent drift: Models linear bias variation driven by ambient temperature changes.
- Vibration noise: Superimposes high-frequency sinusoidal components arising from mechanical thruster and actuator vibrations.

In Section III-A, to validate the model, an Allan variance analysis was performed using over 9 hours of static data captured from a real tactical-grade IMU, the JIMS-80. Allan variance allows separating short-term noise (Angle Random Walk: ARW) from long-term drift (Bias Instability: BI).

As a result, the conventional Stonefish model (dashed red line in Fig. F3) was dominated by white noise with an ARW of approximately $1.6\times 10^{-3}$ rad/s, exhibiting an unrealistic response devoid of bias instability. In contrast, the proposed model (solid blue line) achieved an ARW of around $5\times 10^{-4}$ rad/s while clearly exhibiting a bias instability valley in the $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-6}$ rad/s region, aligning remarkably well with the stochastic structure of the real JIMS-80 (solid green line).

captions.F3: Allan deviation comparison between the real IMU (JIMS-80, solid green), the proposed IMU model (solid blue), and the legacy IMU model (dashed red). The horizontal axis shows integration time $\tau$, and the vertical axis shows gyro (top) and accelerometer (bottom) deviations. While the legacy model exhibits purely monotonically decreasing white noise, the new model captures the upturn caused by long-term bias instability, matching the real device.

sections.heading: Beam-level modeling and long-term drift in DVLs
sections.summary: For Doppler Velocity Logs (DVLs) measuring bottom and water velocities, the authors implemented velocity projection across four acoustic beams coupled with a random-walk bias accumulation model. In a 3-hour static test, while the legacy model unrealistically suppressed error due to white noise cancellation, the new model reproduced monotonic drift accumulation (0.56 m/h) matching real hardware.
sections.details:
Doppler Velocity Logs (DVLs) are essential underwater navigation sensors that estimate a vehicle's velocity relative to the seafloor or surrounding water mass by measuring the Doppler shift of reflected acoustic pulses. Whereas legacy Stonefish relied on an ad-hoc drift rate parameter, this study introduces physically grounded beam-level measurements and long-term bias modeling.

In bottom tracking, the true vehicle velocity relative to the seabed, $\mathbf{v}_{\text{true}}$, is projected onto four acoustic beam direction vectors $\mathbf{d}_i$, each tilted at an angle $\theta$ from the vertical, adding per-beam white noise $\delta v_i$. Water tracking accounts for local seawater current velocity $\mathbf{v}_{\text{water}}$.

Crucially, the model introduces a slowly time-varying bias vector $\mathbf{b}(t)$. By modeling it as a random walk driven by small random increments, it generates realistic navigation errors upon integration.

In the 3-hour static test shown in Fig. F4, both models showed near-zero mean velocity errors (legacy: $7.0\times 10^{-6}$ m/s, proposed: $2.8\times 10^{-5}$ m/s) and identical short-term noise standard deviations of about $0.02$ m/s. However, when dead reckoning was performed by integrating velocity into position, the legacy white noise model canceled out positive and negative errors, yielding an unrealistically small drift of only $0.21$ m/h. In contrast, the proposed model avoided artificial cancellation and accumulated a realistic, monotonically growing position drift of $0.56$ m/h characteristic of real DVL units.

captions.F4: Comparison of DVL velocity time series (left) and dead-reckoned position drift (right) during a 3-hour static test. While short-term velocity noise is virtually identical between legacy and proposed models, the legacy model (blue) severely underestimates accumulated position error due to noise cancellation, whereas the proposed model (orange) reveals realistic, prominent drift.

sections.heading: Accurately handling geomagnetic distortion and magnetic disturbances
sections.summary: The authors implemented a magnetometer sensor calculating true local geomagnetic vectors and inclination based on the World Magnetic Model (WMM/IGRF) according to latitude, longitude, and altitude. Modeling hard-iron bias from vehicle ferromagnetism and soft-iron distortion from surrounding materials drastically eliminates the periodic, heading-dependent yaw errors seen in naive fixed-vector models.
sections.details:
Magnetometers (compasses) are critical for estimating an underwater robot's heading (yaw), but Earth's magnetic field is non-uniform. Furthermore, ferromagnetic components inside the vehicle (motors, batteries) and surrounding metal structures heavily distort the local magnetic field. Existing simulators such as HoloOcean merely add noise to a static global magnetic vector, ignoring inclination changes across latitudes and local distortions.

In this work, the local true geomagnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}_{\text{WMM}}$ is computed from latitude, longitude, altitude, and date using the World Magnetic Model (WMM) or International Geomagnetic Reference Field (IGRF). On top of this, the model applies fixed ferromagnetic bias (hard-iron disturbance $\mathbf{B}_{\text{HI}}$) and induced distortion from surrounding magnetic materials (soft-iron matrix $\mathbf{S}$), before transforming the vector into the sensor frame via vehicle attitude $\mathbf{R}_{\text{sensor}}$.

Fig. F5 evaluates tilt-compensated compass yaw estimation along a 3D trajectory of an AUV at latitude 45°. A simplified model (green line) that ignores magnetic dip and hard/soft-iron effects experiences severe distortion when projecting the field onto the horizontal plane, causing periodic estimation errors exceeding $\pm 13^\circ$ depending on heading (orange line). In contrast, the proposed method (blue line) correctly models disturbances and geometric transformations, keeping estimation errors consistently near zero (< $1^\circ$) regardless of orientation.

captions.F5: Magnetometer-only heading estimation (left) and estimation error (right) for an AUV at latitude 45°. The simplified model (green/orange) incurs large periodic errors due to projecting inclination and disturbances onto the horizontal plane. The proposed full model (blue) eliminates systematic bias, keeping error close to zero.

sections.heading: Integrating higher-order hydrodynamics and seafloor terramechanics
sections.summary: Extending Stonefish's local hydrodynamic calculations across surface mesh faces, this work incorporates angle-of-attack lift, spin-induced Magnus effect, Coriolis forces from coupled body-Earth rotations, and depth-dependent density/added-mass variations across pycnoclines down to 1,000 m. Furthermore, Bekker-theory terramechanics enables seafloor crawler simulation.
sections.details:
Buoyancy, quadratic drag, and constant added mass alone cannot account for complex deep-sea vehicle motions. Stonefish integrates hydrodynamic forces across every triangular face of a vehicle's surface mesh. Leveraging this unique strength, the authors added several sophisticated physical models:

- Deep-sea density gradients and added mass variations: A linear model captures the up to 0.3% seawater density increase across the pycnocline down to roughly 1,000 m depth. Furthermore, volumetric compression of both fluid and vehicle structures under extreme hydrostatic pressure is computed using bulk modulus $K$, updating translational added mass $\mathbf{M}_a(d)$ and rotational added inertia $\mathbf{I}_a(d)$ in real time as depth increases.
- Lift and Magnus effect: Lift is computed on each mesh face from local relative flow velocity and angle of attack. Additionally, a distributed Magnus force calculation accounts for vehicle spin. As shown in Fig. F7, this faithfully reproduces the helical lateral trajectory of a lander free-falling to 3,000 m depth—an effect driven by coupling between subtle body rotation and hydrodynamic forces, matching CFD and field trials.
- Coriolis force: Rigid-body inertial forces arising from coupled vehicle translation and rotation are incorporated. As shown in Fig. F6, a straight 100 m traverse produces approximately 0.5 m of lateral drift, enhancing long-distance trajectory prediction.

In Section VI-A, to model seafloor exploration crawlers and lander touchdown dynamics, a terramechanics model based on classical Bekker theory was integrated. Normal pressure $p_s(z) = (k_c / \sqrt{A} + k_\phi) z^n$ is computed from penetration depth $z$ into the terrain mesh face. Tangential maximum shear strength $\tau_{\max} = c + p_s(z) \tan\phi$ is governed by the Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion using soil cohesion $c$ and internal friction angle $\phi$. Adding velocity-proportional normal damping ensures numerically stable contact dynamics. As shown in Fig. F8, crawler launch dynamics realistically show tractive forces exceeding resistance during acceleration before balancing out at steady-state speed.

captions.F7: Horizontal plane (XY) trajectory (left) and yaw variation with depth (right) of a deep-sea lander in free fall down to 3,000 m. While a drag-only model (red line) descends vertically in a straight path, the model incorporating lift and Magnus effects (blue line) exhibits periodic spiraling and lateral translation caused by flow-rotation coupling, consistent with CFD and sea trials.

sections.heading: Fast loading of massive meshes and specialized deep-sea optical simulation
sections.summary: An optimized loader ingests GLTF/GLB 3D models with millions of polygons in seconds, while an OpenGL camera pipeline implements OpenCV-compatible lens distortion. Coupling with the 'DeepSea' optical renderer via ROS accurately reproduces artificial light scattering and turbidity attenuation in total darkness.
sections.details:
Validating perception algorithms demands realistic environmental geometry and accurate camera models. This section details extensions to asset handling and the rendering pipeline.

- Section VII-A (3D Model Loading): To accelerate scene creation, support for GLTF and binary GLB files was introduced. By optimizing scene-graph traversal and allocating memory for vertices, normals, and UV coordinates in a single pass, massive seafloor terrain models containing millions of triangles load in just a few seconds (Fig. F10).
- Section VII-B (Parametric Camera Model): To directly utilize real underwater camera calibration data, an internal OpenGL pipeline applies OpenCV radial distortion coefficients ($k_1, k_2, k_3$) and tangential distortion coefficients ($p_1, p_2$). This enables real-time generation of barrel and pincushion distortions typical of wide-angle and fisheye lenses.
- Section VII-C (Deep-Sea Rendering Integration): Stonefish's built-in renderer was based on the Jerlov water model for sunlit shallow waters. In the deep sea, however, sunlight is zero, and vehicle-mounted artificial lights scattering and attenuating through suspended particles dominate perception. The authors integrated Stonefish with 'DeepSea', an external renderer specialized in deep-ocean radiative transfer, via a ROS image transport bridge. DeepSea takes Stonefish's RGB and depth buffers, applies artificial light attenuation and backscatter phase functions (e.g., Fournier-Forand scattering for marine snow), and republishes the result. This delivers highly realistic deep-sea imagery without compromising physical simulation performance (Fig. F9).

captions.F9: Comparison of camera lens distortion and deep-sea rendering outputs. From left to right: original image, barrel distortion, pincushion distortion, standard Stonefish shallow-water rendering, and the rightmost/bottom rows showing deep-sea imagery generated via DeepSea integration with artificial light attenuation and water-mass scattering (Fournier-Forand scattering, etc.).

sections.heading: Beyond visuals: how physics-driven simulation shapes the future of underwater robotics
sections.summary: This work advocates a paradigm shift from graphics-centric shallow-water simulation to physics-grounded deep-sea simulation spanning dynamics, sensors, and environmental factors. Unifying AUVs, ROVs, landers, and crawlers under one framework greatly advances long-duration navigation, autonomous perception AI, and underwater digital twins.
sections.details:
The core message of this paper is that 'realism' in underwater robotics simulation must pivot from visual surface aesthetics (graphics) to the fidelity of physical phenomena and sensor measurements that directly dictate vehicle motion and localization.

The extended Stonefish simulator accommodates diverse marine robotic platforms—including deep-diving AUVs/ROVs, free-falling landers, seabed crawlers, ASVs (Autonomous Surface Vehicles), and gliders—within a single unified physical framework. In particular, for long-duration navigation benchmarks in GPS-denied environments and for training machine learning/reinforcement learning autonomy under harsh visual constraints, this framework substantially narrows the Sim-to-Real gap caused by non-physical simulator artifacts.

Looking ahead, the authors envision evolving this platform into a full 'deep-sea digital twin' by integrating platform-specific system identification data and empirical oceanographic field models, providing a practical foundation to propel marine robotics research forward.

takeaways: In underwater simulation realism, physical and sensor fidelity—such as IMU/DVL stochastic drift and higher-order hydrodynamics—is far more critical for autonomous navigation than shallow-water lighting effects.

Allan variance analysis is essential for evaluating IMU models; simplistic white noise models miss the long-term bias instability inherent to real MEMS sensors, producing overly optimistic navigation estimates.
For free-falling landers or spinning submersibles, capturing characteristic helical lateral drift requires modeling mesh-level lift, Magnus effects, and Coriolis forces alongside basic drag.
Applying Bekker's terramechanics model across surface mesh faces enables real-time crawler locomotion and touchdown simulation seamlessly coupled with hydrodynamic and buoyancy forces.
limitations: Optical transmission effects through pressure-housing viewports (flat or dome ports)—such as refraction and depth/pressure-dependent non-central projections—are approximated via OpenCV distortion rather than explicitly ray-traced.
Complex fluid-structure interactions (full turbulence and vortex wake interference with vehicle structures) and complete oceanographic environmental stochasticity are not yet fully captured.
The GLTF/GLB loader currently focuses on geometric mesh parsing; full support for Physically Based Rendering (PBR) materials remains an area for future work.
